# Epistle of Barnabas — Chapter 5 (SOPHIA Consensus)

**Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas 5
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Consensus Translation

1. For to this end the Lord endured to deliver his flesh to destruction, that through the remission of sins we might be sanctified — that is, through his blood of sprinkling.
2. For the scripture that concerns him has things partly about Israel and partly about us; and it speaks thus: "He was wounded on account of our transgressions and weakened on account of our sins; by his bruise we were healed. As a sheep he was led to slaughter, and as a lamb silent before its shearer."
3. We ought therefore to give great thanks to the Lord that he has revealed to us things past, given us wisdom concerning things present, and has not left us without understanding in respect of things to come.
4. But the scripture says: "It is not unjust to spread nets for birds." This means that a person who has full knowledge of the way of righteousness and yet diverts himself into the way of darkness will justly perish.
5. There is yet more, brothers: if the Lord endured to suffer for our souls — he who is Lord of the whole world, to whom God said at the foundation of the world, "Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness" — how is it that he endured to suffer at the hands of human beings?
6. Learn! The prophets, having received grace from him, prophesied about him. But he himself — in order to destroy death and to demonstrate the resurrection of the dead — endured to be manifested in flesh, that he might both fulfil to our fathers the promise and, while he was preparing a new people for himself, show while on earth that after raising the dead he will himself execute judgment.
7. Furthermore, teaching Israel and performing such great signs and wonders, he preached to them and loved them greatly.
8. But when he chose his own apostles who were to proclaim his gospel — they were sinners beyond all measure — in order to show that he did not come to call the righteous but sinners; then he revealed himself to be the Son of God.
9. For if he had not come in flesh, how would human beings have been able to look upon him and be saved? Since in beholding the sun, which is the work of his hands and will at last cease to be, they are unable to gaze into its beams.
10. Therefore the Son of God came in flesh for this reason: to sum up the full measure of sins against those who persecuted his prophets to death.
11. To this end, therefore, he endured. For God says the affliction of his flesh is from them: "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered."
12. He himself willed to suffer thus, because it was necessary for him to suffer upon a tree. For the prophet says about him: "Spare my soul from the sword" and "Pierce my flesh with nails, for assemblies of evildoers have risen against me."
13. And again he says: "Behold, I have given my back to the smiters and my cheeks to blows, and I set my face as a firm rock."

---

## Council Notes

- v.2: Isaiah 53:5, 7 (LXX). One of the earliest systematic christological readings of the Suffering Servant.
- v.5: The creation formula ("Let us make") from Genesis 1:26 is used as evidence of Christ's pre-existence and divine identity — the same move as John 1:1-3 and Proverbs 8, but more explicitly tied to the Incarnation.
- v.8: "Sinners beyond all measure" — the apostles' sinfulness is theologically significant for Barnabas: it demonstrates the inclusive scope of Christ's mission. This is a distinctive reading that goes further than Mark 2:17.
- v.10: "Sum up the full measure of sins" — this is a fulfillment theology: Christ's death was timed for when Israel's sins against the prophets had reached their maximum measure (cf. Matthew 23:32; 1 Thess 2:16).
- v.12: "Suffer upon a tree" — *xylon* — the cross as tree, echoing Deuteronomy 21:23 / Galatians 3:13. Barnabas makes the tree-cross typology explicit.
